CPT Code(s): {{cpt_codes}}
ICD-10 Code(s): {{icd_codes}}

Dear Medical Director / Utilization Review Committee,

I am writing to formally appeal the denial of prior authorization for bariatric / metabolic surgery for my patient. This procedure is medically necessary and is supported by the 2022 American Society for Metabolic and Bariatric Surgery (ASMBS) / International Federation for the Surgery of Obesity and Metabolic Disorders (IFSO) Indications for Metabolic and Bariatric Surgery, multiple randomized controlled trials, and your plan's stated coverage criteria.

BMI Classification: [BMI Category]
Recommended Procedure: [Procedure]
Expected Metabolic Benefit: [Expected Benefit]

This patient has a BMI of [BMI] kg/m² ([WEIGHT] lbs, height [HEIGHT]), meeting criteria for [Class III / Class II] obesity. The patient has the following obesity-related comorbidities:
• [LIST COMORBIDITIES: T2DM, HTN, OSA, dyslipidemia, GERD, osteoarthritis, etc.]

These comorbidities are directly attributable to obesity and are expected to improve significantly or resolve following bariatric surgery.

EVIDENCE-BASED JUSTIFICATION:

1. 2022 ASMBS/IFSO GUIDELINE SUPPORT:
Per the 2022 ASMBS/IFSO Indications for Metabolic and Bariatric Surgery (Eisenberg D, et al., Surg Obes Relat Dis 2022;18:1345-1356), bariatric surgery is indicated for:
• BMI ≥40 kg/m² regardless of comorbidities (Class I recommendation)
• BMI ≥35 kg/m² with at least one obesity-related comorbidity (Class I recommendation)
• BMI ≥30 kg/m² with metabolic disease (T2DM, metabolic syndrome) — expanded 2022 indication

This patient meets criteria [SPECIFY WHICH CRITERION].

2. RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL EVIDENCE:
The STAMPEDE trial (Schauer PR, et al., NEJM 2017;376:641-651) demonstrated that bariatric surgery was significantly superior to intensive medical therapy for glycemic control in T2DM patients with BMI ≥27, with 29% achieving T2DM remission at 5 years vs 5% with medical therapy.

The Swedish Obese Subjects (SOS) study (Sjöström L, et al., JAMA 2012;307:56-65) demonstrated a 40% reduction in cardiovascular events and significant reduction in all-cause mortality in patients who underwent bariatric surgery compared to matched controls.

3. LONG-TERM OUTCOMES:
Adams et al. (NEJM 2007;357:753-761) demonstrated a 40% reduction in all-cause mortality at 7 years following gastric bypass surgery compared to non-surgical controls, with significant reductions in cancer-related and cardiovascular mortality.

RISK OF DENIAL:
Without bariatric surgery, this patient will continue to experience progressive obesity-related complications including [DESCRIBE: worsening T2DM, cardiovascular risk, OSA, joint deterioration, etc.]. The long-term costs of untreated morbid obesity — including hospitalizations, medications, and disability — significantly exceed the one-time cost of bariatric surgery.
